Recent findings on vector vortex-bearing light beams can be understood within the broader framework of geometric phases in optics. In this interpretation, the spatially varying polarization of an inhomogeneous beam causes its local polarization basis to undergo geometric evolution. The resulting spin-redirection phase produces an effective circular birefringence, which is proposed as the physical origin of the topological phase singularities observed in such polarization patterns.

This geometric-phase perspective provides a unified explanation for a range of recent experimental observations and theoretical predictions concerning vector vortex beams. Rather than treating polarization structure, phase singularities, and angular momentum conversion as separate phenomena, it connects them through the geometry of the beam’s evolving polarization state. In particular, the shift in a light beam’s orbital angular momentum can be identified with the angular-momentum holonomy associated with the accumulated geometric phase. Thus, changes in orbital angular momentum emerge naturally as a global consequence of the beam’s local geometric evolution.

Geometric-phase optics provides a unified framework for understanding the polarization structure and phase topology of vector vortex beams. Unlike uniformly polarized scalar beams, vector vortex beams possess spatially varying states of polarization, so their evolution must be described in terms of both spin and orbital degrees of freedom. When the local propagation direction or polarization basis changes across the beam, the polarization vector undergoes parallel transport on the appropriate geometric-state space. This transport produces a spin-redirection geometric phase whose sign depends on the helicity of the circular-polarization component. The resulting helicity-dependent phase may be interpreted as an effective circular birefringence, even when it originates from geometry rather than from conventional material anisotropy.

Within this picture, the inhomogeneous polarization pattern of a vector vortex beam is decomposed into right- and left-circularly polarized components. Because these components acquire geometric phases of opposite sign, they develop different azimuthal phase factors. At points where the polarization state becomes undefined or where one component vanishes, these phase factors generate topological singularities. The corresponding winding numbers are therefore not introduced independently; they arise naturally from the geometric evolution of the beam’s spin state. Polarization singularities and optical vortices can thus be regarded as observable manifestations of the spin-redirection phase.

The same geometric phase also explains changes in the beam’s orbital angular momentum. An azimuthally varying phase of the form \(\exp(i\ell\phi)\) carries an orbital angular momentum of \(\ell\hbar\) per photon. When geometric transport contributes an additional winding to this phase, the orbital-angular-momentum index is shifted by an amount determined by the geometric-phase holonomy accumulated around a closed path. In other words, the net change in orbital angular momentum is exactly equivalent to the angular-momentum holonomy associated with the geometric phase. This equivalence expresses angular-momentum conservation while clarifying how spin-dependent geometric evolution is converted into orbital structure.

The framework therefore connects three features that are often treated separately: spatially varying polarization, topological phase singularities, and spin-to-orbital angular-momentum conversion. By identifying spin-redirection-phase-induced circular birefringence as their common geometric origin, it provides a coherent interpretation of vector vortex beams and supports the view that their singularities are generated by polarization-dependent geometric transport rather than by an unrelated dynamical phase.

## Recent Developments in Angular and OAM

Recent versions of **Angular** have introduced improvements in performance, developer experience, and application architecture. Features such as standalone components, signals, improved server-side rendering, and faster build tools make it easier to create scalable, responsive web applications.

When Angular applications are deployed to cloud environments, **OAM**—the **Open Application Model**—can help standardize their operational configuration. Developers can package an Angular front end as a containerized component, while operations teams use OAM definitions to manage deployment policies, scaling, networking, and environment-specific settings.

Combining recent Angular capabilities with OAM creates a clear separation between application development and infrastructure management. Angular provides the framework for building modern user interfaces, while OAM offers a consistent model for deploying and operating those applications across cloud platforms.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize recent findings on vector vortex-bearing light beams and propose a unified geometric-phase interpretation of their inhomogeneous polarization patterns.
counterfactuals.output:
## Recent picture of vector vortex beams

Vector vortex-bearing beams combine an optical phase singularity with a spatially varying polarization state. Unlike scalar vortex beams, they generally cannot be written as one spatial mode times one fixed Jones vector. A useful minimal representation is

\[
\mathbf E(r,\phi)=
a(r)e^{i\ell_{+}\phi}\,|R\rangle+
b(r)e^{i\ell_{-}\phi+i\delta(r,\phi)}\,|L\rangle ,
\]

where \(|R\rangle\) and \(|L\rangle\) are circular-polarization states and \(\ell_\pm\) are orbital-angular-momentum charges.

Recent work has converged on several themes:

- **Compact generation and conversion.** q-plates, patterned liquid crystals, dielectric metasurfaces, geometric-phase holograms, and integrated devices now generate vector vortices with high efficiency and programmable radial, azimuthal, hybrid, and full-Poincaré textures.
- **Topological polarization structures.** Polarization maps are increasingly described as optical merons, skyrmions, Möbius-like textures, and lattices of polarization singularities. Their integer or half-integer indices can remain stable even when the detailed intensity and ellipticity distributions are distorted.
- **Spin–orbit interaction.** Focusing, propagation through anisotropic media, interfaces, and scattering couple helicity to orbital phase. This produces longitudinal fields, transverse spin, spin-dependent shifts, and conversion between polarization and vortex singularities.
- **Generalized Poincaré-sphere descriptions.** Hybrid-order and higher-order Poincaré spheres organize superpositions of opposite helicities carrying different OAM. They make clear that many apparently distinct vector beams are different trajectories or surfaces in one spin–orbit state space.
- **Beyond monochromatic paraxial beams.** Current studies extend these concepts to tightly focused, pulsed, partially coherent, nonlinear, and spatiotemporal fields, where polarization can vary in three spatial dimensions or across space and time.
- **Quantum and information applications.** The nonseparability of polarization and spatial mode—often called classical entanglement—supports high-dimensional encoding, metrology, imaging, and quantum-state interfaces. The same structures are useful for mode-selective communication and enhanced sensing.
- **Nonlinear and non-Hermitian settings.** Frequency conversion, gain/loss, and topological photonic systems can transfer, reshape, or selectively amplify vector-vortex topology, although conservation laws depend on symmetry and phase matching.

## A unified geometric-phase interpretation

The polarization pattern is governed primarily by the **relative phase** between the two spin components. From the field above,

\[
S_1+iS_2
=2a^*b\,
e^{i[(\ell_- -\ell_+)\phi+\delta]},
\qquad
S_3=|a|^2-|b|^2 ,
\]

so the polarization-ellipse orientation is

\[
\psi(r,\phi)
=\frac12\arg(S_1+iS_2)
=\frac12\left[(\ell_- -\ell_+)\phi+\delta(r,\phi)\right].
\]

Thus a vortex-phase difference becomes a rotation of the local polarization ellipse. Around a closed loop, its index is

\[
I=\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint d\psi
=\frac{\ell_- -\ell_+}{2}
+\frac{1}{4\pi}\oint d\delta .
\]

This directly explains integer and half-integer polarization defects.

### Geometric formulation

Normalize the local Jones vector,

\[
|u(\mathbf r)\rangle=
\frac{\mathbf E(\mathbf r)}
{\sqrt{\mathbf E^\dagger\mathbf E}},
\]

and regard it as a point on the Poincaré sphere. The beam then defines a map

\[
\mathbf r\longmapsto \mathbf s(\mathbf r),
\]

from real space to polarization-state space. Its Berry connection and curvature are

\[
\mathbf A=i\langle u|\nabla u\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf F=\nabla\times\mathbf A.
\]

For a closed spatial contour \(C\), the polarization state traces a contour on the Poincaré sphere and acquires the Pancharatnam–Berry phase

\[
\gamma_{\rm g}
=\oint_C\mathbf A\cdot d\mathbf r
=-\frac{\Omega_C}{2},
\]

up to sign and gauge convention, where \(\Omega_C\) is the enclosed solid angle.

This suggests the following unified statement:

> An inhomogeneous polarization pattern is the real-space image of a spatially varying spinor whose relative spin–orbit phase produces a trajectory on the Poincaré sphere; the associated polarization winding, singularities, and topological charge are holonomies or curvature integrals of that state-space map.

It unifies several familiar cases:

- **Radial and azimuthal beams:** the local state runs around the Poincaré equator while encircling the beam axis.
- **Full-Poincaré beams:** radius and azimuth together cover a finite fraction, often nearly all, of the sphere.
- **q-plates and geometric-phase metasurfaces:** a local optic-axis angle \(\alpha(\mathbf r)\) gives opposite helicities phases \(\pm2\alpha\), creating the required relative phase and OAM shift.
- **Skyrmion or meron textures:** the normalized Stokes field carries a real-space topological density
  \[
  \rho_{\rm top}
  =\frac{1}{4\pi}
  \mathbf s\cdot
  (\partial_x\mathbf s\times\partial_y\mathbf s),
  \]
  which is the pullback of the Poincaré-sphere area form and therefore closely related to Berry curvature.
- **Tight focusing and propagation:** local changes in the propagation frame parallel-transport the polarization basis, adding a geometric contribution to the relative phase and generating spin–orbit conversion.

## Important qualification

Not every spatial phase in a vector beam is geometric. The total relative phase should be separated as

\[
\Delta\Phi
=
\Delta\Phi_{\rm dyn}
+\Delta\Phi_{\rm geom}
+\Delta\Phi_{\rm prop},
\]

where the terms arise from optical path or material retardance, Pancharatnam–Berry evolution, and propagation or focusing. Only closed-loop phases or gauge-invariant curvature quantities permit an unambiguous geometric interpretation.

Accordingly, the most general framework is not that every polarization texture *is* a geometric phase, but that its observable winding is determined by the gauge-invariant holonomy of the local polarization spinor, with dynamical phase acting as an additional deformation. This framework covers conventional vector vortices, full-Poincaré beams, metasurface-generated fields, and optical skyrmions within the same geometry.

counterfactuals.prompt: How can the spin redirection phase explain topological singularities and orbital angular momentum shifts in vector vortex beams?
counterfactuals.output:
The **spin-redirection phase** is a geometric, or Berry, phase acquired when the propagation direction \(\mathbf{k}\) of a circularly polarized field changes. It connects three features of vector vortex beams: spatially varying polarization, phase singularities, and spin-to-orbital angular-momentum conversion.

### 1. Geometric phase from redirecting the wavevector

For helicity \(\sigma=\pm1\), transporting the local polarization basis around a closed path on the wavevector sphere gives

\[
\gamma_\sigma=-\sigma\Omega,
\]

where \(\Omega\) is the solid angle enclosed by that path. For wavevectors lying on a cone of polar angle \(\theta\),

\[
\gamma_\sigma=-2\pi\sigma(1-\cos\theta),
\]

up to sign conventions for helicity and azimuth.

Thus, even if the original scalar field has no azimuthal phase, a spatially dependent propagation direction can produce a phase factor of the form

\[
e^{i\Delta \ell\,\phi},
\qquad
\Delta \ell=\sigma(1-\cos\theta).
\]

This azimuthal geometric phase is interpreted as an orbital angular momentum shift.

### 2. Origin of topological singularities

A vector vortex beam has a polarization basis that rotates around its axis. The circular polarization components acquire opposite geometric phases,

\[
E_\sigma(\rho,\phi)\propto A_\sigma(\rho)e^{i\ell_\sigma\phi}.
\]

At the beam axis, \(\phi\) is undefined. If \(\ell_\sigma\neq0\), regularity requires the corresponding amplitude to vanish there. The axis therefore becomes a phase singularity or a polarization singularity.

Geometrically, this occurs because a helicity basis cannot be chosen smoothly over the entire \(\mathbf{k}\)-sphere. Its Berry curvature is equivalent to that of a monopole at \(\mathbf{k}=0\). The resulting phase winding is therefore topological: it cannot be removed by a smooth local redefinition of phase without moving or annihilating singularities of opposite charge.

### 3. Orbital angular momentum shift

Suppose an input paraxial beam has vortex charge \(\ell\) and helicity \(\sigma\). After redirection through an angle \(\theta\), its spin projected on the fixed \(z\)-axis changes from

\[
S_z=\sigma\hbar
\quad\text{to}\quad
S_z=\sigma\hbar\cos\theta.
\]

Conservation of total angular momentum then requires

\[
\langle L_z\rangle
=
\hbar\left[\ell+\sigma(1-\cos\theta)\right].
\]

Hence

\[
\Delta L_z=\sigma\hbar(1-\cos\theta),
\]

which is precisely the shift associated with the spin-redirection phase. In a nonparaxial or tightly focused beam, this appears component-wise as integer-charge vortices, typically with azimuthal orders

\[
\ell,\qquad \ell+\sigma,\qquad \ell+2\sigma
\]

for the same-helicity transverse, longitudinal, and opposite-helicity components, respectively, with convention-dependent signs. Their weighted average gives the possibly noninteger expectation value above.

In short, **the varying propagation direction creates a helicity-dependent Berry phase; its azimuthal winding generates topological singularities, while its phase gradient transfers angular momentum from spin to orbital motion without changing total angular momentum.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper abstract arguing that circular birefringence induced by the spin redirection phase is responsible for polarization singularities in vector vortex beams.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—**Polarization singularities in vector vortex beams are commonly described through spatially varying superpositions of spin and orbital angular-momentum states, yet the geometric mechanism governing their formation remains debated. Here, we argue that these singularities originate from an effective circular birefringence induced by the spin-redirection geometric phase. When the local propagation direction varies across a structured optical field, parallel transport of the polarization state produces helicity-dependent geometric phases. Their spatially varying phase difference acts as a geometric circular birefringence, driving the local polarization through distinct trajectories on the Poincaré sphere. Using a Jones-field description combined with Berry-phase transport, we show that zeros of the polarization components and the associated C-points, L-lines, and polarization-index structure occur where this helicity-dependent phase retardation satisfies singularity conditions. The predicted singularity positions and topological indices are determined by the beam’s angular-spectrum geometry and vortex charge rather than by material anisotropy. This framework unifies spin–orbit coupling, geometric-phase accumulation, and polarization-singularity formation in vector vortex beams, and distinguishes spin-redirection-induced birefringence from conventional circular birefringence arising from optical activity. The results provide a geometric interpretation of polarization topology and suggest routes for controlling singularity networks through wavefront shaping and nonparaxial beam engineering.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a technical paragraph connecting geometric phase, spin redirection, circular birefringence, topological phase singularities, and angular momentum holonomy in structured optical beams.
counterfactuals.output: In a structured optical beam, the spatial evolution of polarization and propagation direction traces a path on the appropriate Poincaré or momentum-space sphere, generating a geometric phase equal to the associated Berry holonomy. When the local wavevector is redirected, parallel transport of the transverse polarization produces the spin-redirection (Rytov–Vladimirskii–Berry) phase, whose sign depends on helicity; circular birefringence similarly gives opposite phase accumulation to left- and right-circular components through unequal refractive indices. Their interference can imprint azimuthally varying phases on the field, creating polarization or scalar phase singularities around which the phase winds by an integer multiple of \(2\pi\), thereby defining a topological charge. Because this winding couples spin and orbital degrees of freedom, cyclic evolution of the beam’s internal and spatial structure yields an angular-momentum holonomy: after a closed parameter-space loop, the field returns to its local physical configuration while retaining a geometric phase and, where symmetry permits, a corresponding redistribution between spin and orbital angular momentum, with total angular momentum conserved.
